To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) ZIKV infection induces an effector CD8+ T cell response in the CNS that is dependent on the B cell response, (2) ZIKV infected mice have a robust CD8+ T response in the CNS, and (3) ZIKV induced effector CD8 + T cells are capable to control local viral infection.

(i) ZIKV induced effector CD8T cells are capable of controlling viral replication in the brain if they arrive in sufficient numbers and differentiation state, and that (ii) this process is dependent on the presence of B cells.
the effector CD 8 T cells can be protective in the CNS if they arrive early after infection, in sufficient numbers and in a differentiated state.

understanding the role of CD4 and CD8 T cells against ZIKV infection, with the goal of identifying correlates that can be used to improve vaccine design.

the role of CD4 and CD8 T cells during ZIKV infection and the mechanisms by which these cells contribute to the control of viral replication.

the role of CD 8 T cells in controlling Zika virus infection in the CNS is a function of time and numbers, and that a vaccine that is able to induce an early and sufficient CD8 T cell immune response in the brain may provide protection against ZIKV infection.
the effector CD 8 T cell response is an essential component of protective immunity against ZIKV infection.

The main takeaway from our work is that
CD8 T cell responses are important in the context of ZIKV infection and that the timing of their recruitment to the CNS is a critical determinant of their antiviral efficacy.
